opus-5.5.text:
I'd say the difference is less about who's smarter and more about what each ecosystem is good at and what it rewards.

In the US, many leading teams start from the model. They come out of large-model labs or top robotics research groups, and their core belief is that intelligence is the bottleneck. So they put enormous resources into foundation models for robots: vision-language-action models, cross-embodiment training, scaling laws for robot data. The hardware is often treated as a carrier. Sometimes they even use fairly off-the-shelf arms or simple grippers, because they want to prove the "brain" generalizes. Capital there is willing to fund a long, uncertain research path, so you see companies raising huge rounds before they have meaningful revenue.

In China, the starting point is more often the body and the scenario. We have an extraordinary hardware supply chain: motors, reducers, sensors, batteries, structural parts. Iteration on hardware is very fast and very cheap compared with anywhere else. So many Chinese companies first get a humanoid or a quadruped walking, running, doing flips, getting the cost down, and getting units shipped. Then they ask: which scenario can I land in? Factories, logistics, education, research platforms, exhibitions, retail. The pressure to commercialize is stronger, partly because investors here want to see revenue earlier, and partly because the competition is so intense.

Then there's data, where the two sides also diverge. Overseas teams lean heavily on simulation, internet video, and large-scale teleoperation in a fairly centralized way. In China you see more "data factories," big facilities where many operators collect real-world manipulation data, because labor and hardware make that relatively affordable. Each approach has trade-offs: real data is high quality but expensive to scale, while simulation and video scale well but face the sim-to-real gap.

I don't think either route is simply right. If you only build the brain, you can end up with impressive demos that can't be deployed cheaply or reliably. If you only build the body, you get beautiful hardware that can only perform choreographed motions, with no real generalization. Over the next few years I expect the two routes to converge. Chinese companies will invest more in models, and overseas companies will care much more about hardware cost and manufacturability. Whoever closes the loop first wins: real deployments generate data, the data improves the model, and the better model opens up more deployments. That closed loop matters more than which end you started from.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that the routes will converge, with Chinese companies investing more in models and overseas companies focusing more on hardware costs and manufacturability.

r002.rationale: It describes real-world data collection alongside internet video and simulation, but does not say to combine these sources to address a scarcity of real-world data.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention reinforcement learning or identify it as a differentiator among companies using a data-pyramid approach.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss imitation learning or say it can suffice for demonstrations in constrained scenarios.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd frame the difference along three axes: where the data comes from, what the "body" is, and what the company is actually optimizing for.

On data, the leading American efforts, whether it's Tesla with Optimus, Figure, or the Physical Intelligence and Google DeepMind camp, are making a very explicit bet on the scaling hypothesis. The belief is that if you build a big enough foundation model on video, teleoperation data, and internet-scale pretraining, generalization will emerge the way it did in language. So you see enormous investment in teleoperation farms, in simulation, in collecting hundreds of thousands of hours before the robot does anything useful. It's capital-heavy and it's patient. Chinese companies, with a few exceptions, are more pragmatic. The data strategy is usually "put the robot in a real scene early, even if the scene is narrow, and let deployment generate data." Factories, logistics, inspection, exhibitions. You iterate in the field rather than in the lab.

On hardware, this is where China has a structural advantage, and the routes diverge because of it. The supply chain for motors, reducers, lidar, batteries, and joint modules is largely domestic, so companies like Unitree can ship a humanoid at a price point that would be unthinkable in the US, and they can revise the mechanical design every few months. That pushes Chinese teams toward a "hardware-first, iterate fast, sell early" posture. American companies often treat hardware as a means to an end, something you build once so the model has a vessel. They're slower on the body because they're betting the brain is the moat.

On objectives, I'd say the US route is closer to "build AGI with a body." The humanoid is the general-purpose end state and everything is organized around that. In China the question is more often "which industrial problem can a robot close the loop on in the next 18 months." You see more quadrupeds, more wheeled bases, more specialized manipulators, because the form factor follows the use case, not the thesis. The humanoid wave in China is real, but much of it is also driven by local government support and capital markets rather than a purely technical conviction.

Where I think the lines are blurring: Chinese teams are now training their own VLA models and catching up on the algorithm side faster than people expected, partly because open-source releases from the West have compressed the gap. And American companies are discovering they can't ignore cost and manufacturability forever. My honest view is that neither side has proven generalization yet. The US has better models and more compute, China has better bodies and more deployment surface. Whoever marries the two first, and I suspect it will take cross-border supply chains whether anyone likes it or not, wins this cycle.

r002.rationale: It mentions internet-scale pretraining and simulation, but does not say they supplement real-world data to address its scarcity.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not mention reinforcement learning or a shared data-pyramid approach.

r004.rationale: The candidate does not discuss imitation learning, demonstrations, or constrained scenarios.

astra-6.text:
I’d look at this along three dimensions: the hardware, the intelligence model, and the path to commercialization. The distinction isn’t simply China versus abroad; companies within each market can take very different routes.

On hardware, one route is to develop the robot and its intelligence together, while another is to focus on models that can work across different robot bodies. Vertical integration gives you more control over performance, but it also requires substantial investment. A broader model approach has the potential to scale across hardware, but transferring capabilities between robots is difficult.

On intelligence, the key question is how much you build around an end-to-end learned model and how much you retain explicit modules for perception, planning, and control. Those aren’t mutually exclusive. A robot can use a large model to interpret a task while relying on more established control methods to execute movements reliably.

If I had to describe the regional difference, I’d say China’s manufacturing ecosystem makes it attractive to iterate on hardware and pursue concrete deployment scenarios. Some companies abroad put more emphasis on general-purpose models and the data infrastructure needed to train them. But I’d treat that as a tendency, not a clean dividing line.

Ultimately, I think the decisive issue is the learning loop: can you deploy the robot, collect useful data from its successes and failures, and turn that data into better performance at an acceptable cost? A compelling demonstration is one thing. Reliable operation in a customer’s environment is a much harder test.

r001.rationale: The response describes regional tendencies and says they are not a clean dividing line, but does not predict that the approaches will converge.

r002.rationale: It discusses collecting deployment data, but does not identify internet or synthetic/simulation data as supplements for scarce real-world data.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention reinforcement learning or identify it as a differentiator among companies using a data-pyramid approach.

r004.rationale: It contrasts demonstrations with reliable deployment, but does not explain that imitation learning can suffice for demos because their scenarios are narrowly constrained.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by saying that the difference isn’t simply that China follows one technical route and companies abroad follow another. The more useful distinction is where a company starts: with the robot hardware, with the underlying AI model, or with a particular application.

A hardware-led team asks, “How do we make the machine move reliably and manufacture it at a reasonable cost?” A model-led team asks, “How do we give the robot capabilities that transfer across tasks?” And an application-led team asks, “What can this robot do for a customer today?” Those starting points lead to different choices about robot design, training data, and how much to rely on learned behavior versus conventional control.

My impression is that Chinese companies often put more emphasis on integrating hardware and software, controlling costs, and getting into real operating environments quickly. Some prominent overseas teams put more emphasis on general-purpose models and learning capabilities that can work across different robots and tasks. But that’s a tendency, not a clean dividing line. You can find both approaches in both places.

The central challenge is the same: how do you turn a successful demonstration into reliable performance when the environment changes? A robot might complete a task once, but can it repeat it, recover from mistakes, and do it at an acceptable cost? I’d judge the technical routes by those questions, rather than by geography alone.

r001.rationale: The response says Chinese and overseas approaches overlap and that the distinction is not a clean dividing line, but it does not predict that their technical approaches will converge.

r002.rationale: It mentions training data generally, but does not identify internet and synthetic or simulation data as supplements for scarce real-world data.

r003.rationale: It contrasts learned behavior with conventional control, but does not identify reinforcement learning as a differentiator among companies using a data-pyramid approach.

r004.rationale: It discusses demonstrations and reliability, but does not explain that imitation learning may suffice for demonstrations because they use narrowly constrained scenarios.
